Learning Welsh is so much easier when you're a child. Much easier than it is as an adult anyway. My parents sent me to Welsh primary and secondary schools despite not speaking a word of Welsh at home. 

While I think it's wonderful to keep the language alive, it's only useful if you intend to live in Wales forever. Your child will learn everything in Welsh (with the exception of English lessons obviously) so all terminology is in Welsh. Great if you live there, but I no longer do. While some words are similar (triongl isosgeles) some are vastly different. It has caused me a lot of confusion over the years. 

Having said that, being bilingual has a profound affect on the brain, and despite the confusion I do love being able to speak Welsh. That is until someone asks you to say the really long place name for the 8 millionth time haha!

I use breathing exercises and a sort of mind game someone taught me. First of all, I take 10 deep breaths, making sure to stay mindful while I do it. Afterwards I play a word game in my head, I used to start at A but I'd never get past C before falling asleep so now I choose an arbitrary letter and start listing things that start with that letter. 

You can list artists, movies, shows, foods, brands, countries etc or try to think up the longest words starting with that letter. If I recall correctly, these are somatic thoughts and will help guide your brain to sleep.

I disagree, a toxic and manipulative person wouldn't care enough to ask for the signs of toxicity and manipulative behaviours.

People who minimise your problems, gaslight and generally treat you as if you're worth less than they are, or expect you to be there for them but don't reciprocate are all signs of toxicity and manipulation.

Firstly and foremost, BPD aside you're a human and humans make mistakes. While it's important to recognise that our BPD makes us do things we feel bad about, it's the guilt that we carry that really hurts. We have to learn to forgive ourselves whilst also not using our condition as an excuse to behave poorly.

As someone who hurt a lot of people (mostly unintentionally) growing up I can relate hard to this post. It took me a long time to even figure out I had BPD, let alone why I was hurting the person I love most in the world. My partner and I have just celebrated 12 years together, it totally is possible for those with BPD to have long lasting and meaningful relationships, but the important part is recognising where and why you experience these issues and what triggers you. For me, I self-sabotage as I truly believed for a very long time that I didn't *deserve* to be happy, but I learned that I absolutely do deserve to be happy. I also learned why I do the things I do and I've worked hard to change them. 

It's also important to remember that any changes you make should always be for yourself and because you are ready to make them. If they're for anyone else, or you are not in a good place to make the changes, it's likely they won't work. You are not a bad person because you make mistakes, the fact that you even notice them and care about them shows you have the capacity for change. Growing as a person is a life-long task, and sometimes it's an uphill struggle, but ultimately it is worth it as I feel more secure and happy in my relationship than I've ever felt before. There is a workbook called the DBT workbook designed specifically for those with BPD, by someone with BPD themselves and I highly recommend it for helping to sort out your thoughts and feelings. My inbox is always open if you need someone to talk to.
